_doc: Live test scenarios: each one is a real chat turn through the whole security layer and the configured model.
role: role id from GET /roles. config (optional): settings applied only for this scenario, then restored:
guardMode (warn|block), maskPii (bool), filters {id: bool}, roles {roleId: [data areas]}, limits {maxPromptChars, maxTurnTokens, maxTurnCost}.
expect: every listed check must hold.
outcome: one of / list of allowed | blocked | denied | redacted  (denied = a tool call was refused or the chatbot refused)
stage: list; at least one verdict or refused tool call comes from one of these controls
contains: list; each item is a string or a list of alternatives that must appear in the reply (numbers match with any separators)
excludes: strings that must not appear in the reply
masked: PII types hidden from the model in the prompt ([] = nothing hidden)
tool: {name, allowed}: the chatbot called this tool (name may be a list) with that result
modelSaw / modelNeverSaw: strings that must / must not appear in what the model received (the user prompt after masking, tool results)
mode (optional): live (default, real model) | mock. A mock scenario needs `model`: the scripted chatbot replies, one step per model call:
{"reply": "text"} or {"tool_calls": [{"name": "tool", "args": {...}}]}. In a reply, {prompt} is the user prompt as the model received it and {tool_result} the last tool result.
Mock runs only the deterministic controls (intent classifier, company policies and the LLM judges are off unless config turns them on).

variants (optional): list of {id, label, config, expect}: the same scenario run once per variant, shown side by side. A variant's config is merged over the scenario's config; its expect replaces the scenario's expect.
Mock scenarios and scenarios with variants run on a copy of the policy for their own turn only: they never change the server's settings.
config.policy (optional): {"controls.pii.threshold": 0.85, ...}: set any key of the policy by its dotted path.
standard (optional): the standard or requirement the scenario illustrates, shown in the interface.
note (optional): an explanation shown next to the scenario, e.g. what switching the control off really changes.

groups.label: Data access by role
groups.description: The same request from different roles: who gets the data and who does not.

groups.label: Reading the database
groups.description: Authorized roles pull real values out of the CSV databases through the tools.

groups.label: Attacks
groups.description: Prompt injection, jailbreaks, impersonation (with guard mode set to block), code execution and PII sent to the model.

groups.label: Block settings
groups.description: The same request under different configurations: each setting changes the result.

groups.label: ON / OFF demonstrations
groups.description: The same situation with one control on and then off, side by side. Scenarios marked mock use a scripted model reply: they show what the layer does with any model output, not how a model behaves.

scenarios.title: Code guard: the model asks to run deserialization code
scenarios.standard: OWASP LLM03 / historical attacks: unsafe deserialization
scenarios.note: Switching the pipeline control off does not strip the protection: the tool's own static check still rejects the payload (a second layer, and a runtime import restriction behind it). What changes is where the attack is stopped and whether the layer reports it: with the control on it is a named, audited decision (attack type Deserialization) before any interpreter touches the code.
